---
title: "11. Range shifts under climate change"
output: rmarkdown::html_vignette
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(eval = FALSE, collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
fig <- function(f) knitr::include_graphics(file.path("figure", f))
```

tidymapr 0.3.0 adds a hybrid model of range shifts: fine-scale climate,
an integrated niche model and a simulation of colonisation and
extinction, run over an ensemble of climate futures. This chapter walks
through it for MacGregor's bowerbird (*Amblyornis macgregoriae*) on Mt
Karimui, Papua New Guinea, with real data: CHELSA climate, GBIF records,
the SRTM elevation model and ESA WorldCover. The figures were made with
the code shown; the code needs an internet connection and is not run
when this page is built.

| Step | Functions |
|---|---|
| Climate for an area, now and in the future | `geo_chelsa_area()`, `geo_chelsa_urls()` |
| Down to the terrain and below the canopy | `geo_downscale_lapse()`, `geo_canopy_offset()` |
| Niche from records and surveys | `sdm_integrated()` |
| Dispersal, colonisation and extinction | `geo_shift_simulate()`, `geo_shift_summary()` |
| Ensembles of futures | `geo_climate_scenarios()`, `geo_shift_ensemble()` |

## 1. Climate for an area

`geo_chelsa_area()` reads CHELSA V2.1 (1981-2010) and CHELSA-CMIP6
projections for five climate models (GCMs), three emission scenarios
(SSPs) and three periods. Only the window over the area is read, so a
region takes seconds.

```{r}
library(tidymapr)
png <- c(143, -8, 147.5, -5)
now <- geo_chelsa_area(png, "bio1")
future <- geo_chelsa_area(png, "bio1",
  period = "2071-2100",
  gcm = c("mpi-esm1-2-hr", "ukesm1-0-ll"), ssp = c("ssp126", "ssp585")
)
warming <- future - now
```

```{r, eval = TRUE, echo = FALSE}
fig("range-cmip6.png")
```

The models disagree: by 2071-2100, central New Guinea warms by about 1
degree C under SSP1-2.6 with MPI-ESM1-2-HR and by over 5 degrees C under
SSP5-8.5 with UKESM1. Projections should span that range.

## 2. Down to the terrain and below the canopy

A 1 km cell on a tropical mountain can span over 1,000 m of elevation,
about 5 degrees C. `geo_downscale_lapse()` corrects each fine cell by its
height above or below the cell's mean, with a lapse rate measured on the
mountain (5.1 degrees C per km on Mt Karimui).

```{r}
area <- c(144.6, -6.7, 145.0, -6.3)
dem <- geo_elevation(bbox = area, buffer = 0)[[1]]
bio1 <- geo_downscale_lapse(geo_chelsa_area(area, "bio1"), dem, lapse_rate = 5.1)
```

```{r, eval = TRUE, echo = FALSE}
fig("range-downscale.png")
```

Below a closed canopy, maximum temperatures are several degrees lower
than in the open. `geo_canopy_offset()` adds that buffer, scaled by
canopy cover.

```{r}
bio5 <- geo_downscale_lapse(geo_chelsa_area(area, "bio5"), dem, 5.1)
trees <- geo_landcover(area, template = dem) == 10
forest_bio5 <- geo_canopy_offset(bio5, terra::resample(trees * 1, dem, "average"), offset = -4)
```

```{r, eval = TRUE, echo = FALSE}
fig("range-canopy.png")
```

## 3. A niche from records and surveys

GBIF records are many but biased towards roads and towns; standardised
surveys are few but unbiased. `sdm_integrated()` fits one niche to both:
presence-only records as a point process and surveys as presence-absence.
Here, 300 GBIF records are combined with the 1965 transect on Mt
Karimui, where the bowerbird was found between 1,585 and 1,981 m.
`unimodal = "bio1"` forces a hump-shaped response to temperature, so the
model cannot predict ever-rising suitability in warmer climates.

```{r}
fit <- sdm_integrated(
  presence = gbif_climate, background = background, area = n_cells,
  survey = transect_1965, covariates = c("bio1", "bio12"), unimodal = "bio1"
)
```

```{r, eval = TRUE, echo = FALSE}
fig("range-response.png")
```

## 4. Dispersal, colonisation and extinction

Suitable climate is not enough: a species has to reach it. 
`geo_shift_simulate()` runs a stochastic patch-occupancy model on a
series of suitability maps. Each generation an empty cell is colonised
with a probability that rises with occupied cells nearby (a negative
exponential dispersal kernel), and an occupied cell persists with a
probability set by its suitability. The model is written in C++ and
runs in parallel; results do not depend on the number of cores.

```{r}
suit <- c(now_suit, suit_2025, suit_2055, suit_2085)
sim <- geo_shift_simulate(suit,
  dispersal_mean = 300, steps_per_layer = 3, nsim = 50, seed = 1
)
geo_shift_summary(sim, elevation = dem)
```

```{r, eval = TRUE, echo = FALSE}
fig("range-simulate.png")
```

```{r, eval = TRUE, echo = FALSE, out.width = "70%"}
fig("range-summary.png")
```

Under SSP5-8.5 with UKESM1 the occupied area first grows from 57 to 90
km^2 as the cooler upper slopes open up, then collapses to 15 km^2 by
2085 as the median elevation climbs from 1,680 to 2,080 m and the range
runs out of mountain.

## 5. Ensembles of futures

`geo_climate_scenarios()` builds every combination of GCM, SSP and lapse
rate on the fine grid; `geo_shift_ensemble()` runs the niche model and
the simulation on each, with limited and unlimited dispersal, and
`summary()` gives the probability of losing more than 30, 50 or 80% of
the range.

```{r}
sc <- geo_climate_scenarios(area, dem,
  variables = c("bio1", "bio12"), period = "2071-2100",
  gcm = c("mpi-esm1-2-hr", "ukesm1-0-ll"), ssp = c("ssp126", "ssp585"),
  lapse_rates = c(4.5, 5.5)
)
ens <- geo_shift_ensemble(fit, sc, dispersal_mean = 300, steps = 8, nsim = 30)
summary(ens)
```

## 6. Does it work? A hindcast

The workflow was tested on birds resurveyed on Mt Karimui in 1965 and
2012 (Freeman and Class Freeman 2014). Using warming measured on the
mountain, the predicted shifts matched the observed community-wide
shifts; see the [full case study](case-karimui-hindcast.html).

```{r, eval = TRUE, echo = FALSE}
fig("range-warming.png")
fig("range-hindcast.png")
```
